field.label: This firewall (these three settings are specific to each firewall; everything below is shared and copied from the active firewall)
Enable HA on this firewall
field.help: Runs the HA service. Turning it off stops heartbeat, replication and automatic failover on this firewall.

field.label: HA link interface (this firewall)
field.help: The dedicated cable to the other firewall. It needs a different static IPv4 address on each firewall and is never put in standby.

field.label: Management interface (this firewall, optional)
field.help: Stays up on the standby, so you can reach its GUI. It also carries a second heartbeat path. It is excluded from MAC sharing and configuration sync.

field.label: Peer port (this firewall)
field.help: TCP port of the secure link between the firewalls, bound to the HA and management address only. Use the same value on both firewalls: it is not copied between them. The firewall rules created by the wizard assume 7690-7691.

field.label: Automatic failover
field.help: The standby takes over by itself when the active firewall is lost. Turn off to switch roles by hand only (a rebooted firewall always waits as standby).

field.label: Peer failure detection time (seconds)
field.help: How long the other firewall must be silent on every heartbeat path before it counts as dead. 1-2 s gives the fastest failover; use 3-5 s on a loaded firewall or a link that is not a dedicated cable, or you risk needless switches.

field.label: Primary takes over again (preemption)
field.help: When the primary firewall is back as standby and the other one has been active and healthy for the delay below, the active role goes back to the primary (a short interruption). Leave off if you prefer to choose the moment yourself.

field.label: Preemption delay (seconds)
field.help: How long the other firewall must have been active and healthy before the role is handed back. Only used when preemption is on.

field.label: Take over when only the HA link says the peer is gone (split-brain risk)
field.help: Without a management interface, the standby normally refuses to take over when it cannot prove that its own HA cable is healthy. Turning this on makes it take over anyway: if only the cable is cut, both firewalls become active. Prefer adding a management interface.

field.label: Monitored interfaces
field.help: If one of these loses its link on the active firewall, the roles are switched after the hold time below, unless the standby reads no link on its own port either (then the outage would only move). A standby keeps its ports down, so its link is usually not readable; that does not prevent the switch. Select every network the firewall must keep serving: with nothing selected a failed network card does not cause a failover. For VLANs on a LAGG select the VLAN interfaces: the LAGG losing all its ports takes them down, while a LAGG that keeps one port does not trigger anything.

field.label: Monitor critical services
field.help: Restarts the packet filter and IPsec if they die on the active firewall; switches roles if that does not help.

field.label: Probe targets (upstream)
field.help: Optional. Up to five IPv4 addresses, comma separated, for example the upstream router. The active firewall pings them every 2 seconds. If none answers for the hold time below and the standby has link on the same ports, the roles are switched. Use addresses that only THIS firewall's uplink can lose: an outage that affects both firewalls cannot be fixed by switching. Switching is suspended for 30 s after every takeover, at most two health switches happen in 30 minutes, and there is a 5 minute cool-down.

field.label: Management probe targets
field.help: Optional. Up to five IPv4 addresses on the management network (the management switch or router). BOTH firewalls ping them from their management address every 2 seconds. A standby that cannot reach them will not take over (it may be the isolated one), and an active firewall will not hand over for a health problem when the standby cannot reach them either. Needs a management interface; use addresses that answer ping.

field.label: Local health-failure hold time (seconds)
field.help: How long a health problem must persist on the active firewall before the roles are switched. A monitored link that lost its carrier counts after a third of it (at least 2 s): a dead card does not come back; services and probe targets use the whole time.

field.label: Keep GUI logins across a failover
field.help: Copies the web GUI sessions of the active firewall to the standby so you stay logged in after a failover. They only travel over the pinned HA connection and are removed on the standby when you log out. Turn off if session data must not leave the active firewall.

field.label: Use a virtual MAC address
field.help: Shared interfaces get a generated MAC address (02:...) instead of the primary's hardware address, so replacing a firewall never changes what the network sees. Applies to interfaces when they are first shared (pairing or kit); addresses already pinned stay as they are.

field.label: Standby mode
field.help: Classic: the standby keeps its data interfaces down; a takeover brings the links up (a real NIC needs seconds to renegotiate). Warm (experimental): the standby keeps the links of its shared interfaces up with its own MAC address, no IP address and IPv6 off, and takes the shared MAC and addresses at takeover. Only interfaces with a static IPv4 address, a shared MAC and a plain NIC or VLAN qualify; the others keep the classic takeover, and any problem falls back to it. Needs a switch that accepts two MAC addresses on the port group and a NIC driver that changes its MAC without dropping the link: validate on your hardware first (docs/fast-ha.md). Hot (experimental): the standby keeps the LAGG, its ports and the VLANs up AND already carrying the shared MAC, with no address and IPv6 off; the takeover only adds the addresses (measured: 120 ms of outage for a client), nothing changes on any link. It watches that the standby never transmits (a device that does is shut down) and that its packet filter has a default deny. Works with failover, load-balance and LACP LAGGs (see the next setting for LACP). Copied from the active firewall: it is the same on both.

field.label: Fast interface takeover
field.help: At a takeover, VLANs with a static IPv4 address (and IP aliases) are brought up with a single ifconfig instead of the PHP interface code, about 2 s faster with 20 VLANs. Anything else (the LAGG, physical NICs, DHCP, IPv6, an MTU, bridges, GRE/GIF, static ARP entries) still uses the stock code, and a VLAN that does not come up as planned falls back to it. Copied from the active firewall.

field.label: Hot standby with an LACP LAGG
field.help: Only for the Hot standby mode and an interface that is directly on a LAGG in LACP mode (VLANs on an unassigned LACP LAGG are always hot). Off: that interface and its VLANs keep the classic takeover. Shared: the standby keeps its LACP bundle established with the shared MAC as system id, so the takeover adds addresses only (fastest). The switch must have one STATIC port-channel per firewall: a switch that aggregates dynamically by the partner system id (some HP/Aruba, Linux-style bonding on the switch side) would merge both firewalls into one LAG. Measured with RouterOS 802.3ad bonds: two separate bonds, both with the shared MAC as partner system id, both fully active. Copied from the active firewall.

field.label: Promiscuous mode on data interfaces
field.help: Needed on virtual NICs (Hyper-V, some virtio setups) whose driver does not reprogram its receive filter when the shared MAC is applied. Real NICs (Intel ixl, igb, ...) do not need it for the shared MAC; a VLAN that carries another MAC than its parent needs it on any NIC, and the daemon then sets it by itself.

field.label: Fencing command
field.help: Absolute path of an executable (owned by root, not writable by others, in directories not writable by others), run before an automatic takeover, for example to power off the peer through IPMI or a smart PDU. Arguments: promote, peer address. A non-zero exit status or a timeout (30 s) CANCELS the takeover, so test it as root first: a failing command disables automatic failover.

field.label: Notification level
field.help: Which events are sent to the webhook. Every event is written to syslog (tag hasyncd). For e-mail, add the HA check to Monit (see the documentation).

field.label: Webhook URL
field.help: Receives a JSON POST ({time, kind, node, role, state, message}) for every event at or above the level. Loopback and link-local addresses are refused.
